1A.6.note: All 112 operations generated from Smithy model via six per-language generators (Go, TypeScript, Ruby, Swift, Kotlin, Rust)

1B.2.note: Service request and response types are generated from the OpenAPI schema in every language, but every language's hand-written magic-link flow builds its own bodies: Go, Swift and Kotlin declare their own shapes (Go's CreateSessionRequest{email} and CreateSessionResponse{message}, where the generated types carry email_address and pending_authentication_token), TypeScript and Ruby build them inline (auth/magic-link.ts, magic_link_flow.rb), and Rust serializes a private Redeem body (magic_link.rs); same root cause as 1C.1 and 1C.3

1B.4.note: Optional fields are optional in TypeScript, Swift and Kotlin, nilable in Ruby and Option in Rust; Go's generated types use plain values with omitempty for every optional field but one (Column.Color is *Color), so an absent field reads as its zero value

1B.5.note: openapi.json types the 29 *_at fields as plain string with no format: date-time; Rust's generator maps every *_at field to chrono::DateTime<Utc> (rust/generator/src/model.rs, rust/fizzy-sdk/src/types.rs), the other languages keep ISO 8601 strings

1C.1.note: Generated service paths match the spec, but the hand-written magic-link flows in Go, TypeScript, Ruby, Swift and Kotlin post to /sessions-style paths the spec does not have (it has /session.json and /session/magic_link.json); only Rust uses the generated routes

1C.3.note: Service paths are generated in every language, but the hand-written magic-link flows in Go (magic_link.go), TypeScript (auth/magic-link.ts), Ruby (magic_link_flow.rb), Swift (Auth/MagicLinkFlow.swift) and Kotlin (auth/MagicLinkFlow.kt) build their own paths rather than using the generated routes; Rust uses routes::CREATE_SESSION and routes::REDEEM_MAGIC_LINK

2A.6.note: Rust keeps a 10 KB prefix of an error body; Go's client reads at most 1 MB and drops a larger one, but its magic-link flow reads up to the 50 MB success limit before checking the status; Ruby skips parsing past 1 MB after Faraday buffers it; TypeScript, Swift and Kotlin read the whole error body with no cap

2D.5.note: Resilience primitives are configurable in every language: Go (WithResilience) and Rust (client builder) apply them per client instance, with circuit breakers and bulkheads keyed by Service.Operation and one rate limiter shared by every operation on the client; TypeScript, Ruby, Swift and Kotlin ship configurable primitives the client does not apply. Retry budgets in Go and Ruby come from the client's max_retries, not the per-operation retry metadata in behavior-model.json

3A.4.note: OAuth PKCE deferred — Fizzy does not implement OAuth

3A.5.note: Keyring storage exists in Go only (go-keyring in go/pkg/fizzy/auth.go); the other five languages have none

3A.6.note: The FIZZY_NO_KEYRING fallback exists in Go only (go/pkg/fizzy/auth.go)

3C.2.note: Success bodies are capped at 50 MB in Go (while reading) and Ruby (after buffering) and at 10 MiB by default in Rust; TypeScript, Swift and Kotlin have no cap

3C.3.note: Messages parsed from a server's error body are truncated to 500 bytes or characters in all six languages (TypeScript, Swift and Kotlin read the full body first; see 3C.2, 2A.6), but not every server-derived or SDK-written message is bounded: TypeScript falls back to the response's statusText untruncated (typescript/src/errors.ts:183), and Go's 404 error quotes the full request URL

3C.4.note: Hooks receive method, URL, attempt and result, never headers, so they cannot log Authorization or Cookie; Go, TypeScript, Ruby and Rust also export header-redaction helpers, which only Rust uses (Response Debug)

4B.5.note: AGENTS.md rule 3 requires unit and conformance tests for every new operation, but the shared fixtures (134 cases across 6 runners: Go, TypeScript, Ruby, Swift, Kotlin, Rust) name 73 of the 112 operations; the other 39 are covered only by family-level path, status, retry, idempotency and security cases

4C.4.note: Go checks for an existing go/ tag and compares the go/ tree; TypeScript and Rust check the registry before publishing (Rust also matches the sha256); Ruby treats an already-pushed error as success; Swift has no publish step. Kotlin treats any 409 in the aggregate publish as success (release-kotlin.yml:84-98), so a rerun after a partial multi-publication upload stops at the first conflict and leaves the rest unpublished
